analysis.one_liner: Restores Clean Water Act protections over all U.S. waters, including wetlands and small streams.
analysis.headline: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee approved the bill, but it never received a Senate floor vote before Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Two Supreme Court decisions narrowed which waters the Clean Water Act protects. This bill rewrote the law to again cover all 'waters of the United States' — including small streams, wetlands, and ponds that feed drinking water supplies — restoring the protections agencies applied before 2001. It kept existing exemptions for normal farming, ranching, and forestry. It passed the Senate environment committee but never came up for a vote by the full Senate before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The more than 110 million people whose public drinking water supplies draw from small or intermittent streams, plus households protected from flooding by wetlands, hunters and anglers who use these waters, and the public generally, since more polluters would need permits before discharging.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drinking-water users, hunters, anglers, flood-prone communities

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the narrower term 'navigable waters' with 'waters of the United States,' defined to include all interstate and intrastate waters, their tributaries, wetlands, and intermittent streams, restoring the scope of protection agencies applied before the 2001 SWANCC and 2006 Rapanos Supreme Court decisions.

The bill's findings state that small and intermittent streams comprise the majority of U.S. stream miles and that source-water areas containing them supply public drinking water systems serving more than 110 million people.
It declares that filling or draining wetlands can cause billions of dollars in flood damage annually, so protecting them aids flood prevention for communities.
It requires the EPA and the Army to write implementing regulations within 18 months of enactment, so the restored protections would take effect on a fixed timetable.

analysis.who_pays: Real estate developers, homebuilders, mining and energy companies, and industrial dischargers, which would need federal permits for more activities near more waters; farmers and ranchers largely avoided new requirements because the bill preserved their existing exemptions.

drawbacks.text: Opponents, including committee Republicans who filed minority views with the report, argued the 'waters of the United States' definition swept too broadly over private land and raised federal permitting burdens and litigation risk for landowners and farmers.

Even with the farming, ranching, and forestry exemptions preserved, the broader definition could mean more permit applications, delays, and costs for anyone building or working near streams and wetlands.

The original draft went further than the version reported to the floor, and the rewrite — which tied jurisdiction to pre-2001 agency rules rather than a maximally broad constitutional claim — came late in the session, leaving little time to resolve disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large and broadly shared: drinking water protection for over 110 million people, wetland flood buffering, and permit requirements for polluters who currently discharge into unprotected small streams. The costs fall mainly on developers, mining, and industrial dischargers, while ordinary farming, ranching, and forestry kept their existing exemptions. The main honest caveat is that a definition this broad does create permitting uncertainty for some private landowners near small waters, and the bill arrived too late in the session to work that out.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved it and put it on the Senate's waiting list in December 2010, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Feingold introduced the bill on April 2, 2009 with 24 original cosponsors — all Democrats or independents, none Republican — and it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

On June 18, 2009 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment, but the formal report did not come until December 10, 2010, when Senator Boxer reported it and minority views were filed.

The reported version had been scaled back from the original draft: instead of claiming the broadest possible constitutional power, it defined covered waters to match pre-2001 agency rules and added exclusions for prior converted cropland and waste treatment systems.
The bill was placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 685) on December 10, 2010 — about three weeks before the Congress ended — and no floor debate or vote ever occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Developers, mining and energy companies, and industrial dischargers are better off, because they never faced the expanded permitting the bill would have required; landowners near small streams also avoided the new federal jurisdiction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Developers, mining firms, and industrial dischargers

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican signed on; committee Republicans filed minority views, and the bill died on a Democrat-led Senate's calendar without a floor vote.

industries.note: Expanded Clean Water Act jurisdiction means more wetland and stream areas require permits before filling or building, raising development costs and delays. Their interest in cheaper land development runs against the water protections the bill would enforce.

The bill expressly preserves the Clean Water Act exemptions for normal farming, ranching, silviculture, agricultural stormwater, irrigated-agriculture return flows, and prior converted cropland, locking in agriculture's carve-outs from the permitting system even as it expands coverage of surrounding waters. Farm groups opposed the bill anyway, fearing the broad definition would later be applied against them.

Some discharges remain exempt (clean stormwater runoff from oil, gas, and mining operations), but other discharges into newly covered small streams would face permitting for the first time. Operating costs rise; cleaner water downstream is the public's offsetting gain.

The bill's findings count roughly 14,800 permitted facilities discharging into small or intermittent streams; many could gain covered-water status only under this bill. New or reissued permits mean compliance spending, while the public gains cleaner streams.
